Clinically sound (proximal myopathy, bruising, plethora and wide purple striae are the discriminating features of cortisol excess). Key was the longest option: shortened. Added Source/sources. Reviewer note: overlaps in theme with parked PAQ15152 (recognise Cushing syndrome) and u74-g02 PAN3639 (proximal myopathy in known Cushing's), but the angle here (which finding discriminates Cushing's from simple obesity) is distinct, so kept.

options.B: Needing to push on his arms to rise from a chair

edits.why_correct: Obesity and hypertension are common and do not distinguish Cushing's syndrome from simple obesity. Features that are more specific for cortisol excess include proximal myopathy, easy bruising, facial plethora and wide purple striae. Needing his arms to stand from a chair indicates proximal muscle weakness and makes testing more worthwhile. Source: NHS, Cushing's syndrome (nhs.uk), reviewed 2025.
edits.correct_answer: B. Needing to push on his arms to rise from a chair

Clinically correct (NICE NG145: if TSH is below range, measure FT4 and FT3). Key was the longest option: reworded all options into a parallel TSH/FT4/FT3 format so the key is no longer longest; why_wrong and exam_trap updated to match.

options.A: Raised TSH with low free T4 and a normal free T3
options.B: Raised TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3
options.C: Normal TSH with normal free T4 and free T3
options.D: Low TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3
options.E: Suppressed TSH with low free T4 and low free T3

edits.why_wrong: A. A raised TSH with a low free T4 is the pattern of primary hypothyroidism. B. A raised TSH with raised free T4 or T3 suggests a rare TSH-secreting pituitary tumour or thyroid hormone resistance, not primary hyperthyroidism. C. Normal results would not explain clinical thyrotoxicosis. E. A low TSH with low free hormones suggests pituitary (secondary) hypothyroidism or non-thyroidal illness, not an overactive gland.
edits.exam_trap: B, Raised TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3 — both values high may seem to fit overactivity, but in primary disease the excess hormone switches TSH off.
edits.why_correct: In primary hyperthyroidism the gland produces excess thyroid hormone, which feeds back on the pituitary and suppresses TSH. The expected pattern is therefore a low TSH with a raised free T4, free T3 or both; occasionally only free T3 is raised (T3 toxicosis). Source: NICE NG145 Thyroid disease: assessment and management, 2019 (updated 2023).
edits.correct_answer: D. Low TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3

issues: Clinically correct: NICE NG145 1.2.8 advises TSH alone first (then FT4 and FT3 if TSH is low), with TRAbs to establish the cause once thyrotoxicosis is confirmed (1.6.1). Only Source/sources added. Reviewer note: u74-g02 PAN8340 tests TSH as the first test for suspected hypothyroidism; different condition so not treated as a repeat, but a reviewer may prefer to keep only one.

edits.why_correct: Her symptoms suggest thyrotoxicosis, and the first step is to confirm thyroid dysfunction with a blood test of TSH, with free T4 and free T3 added if TSH is abnormal. TSH is the most sensitive single test of thyroid status. Tests of cause, such as antibodies or uptake scanning, follow only once thyrotoxicosis is confirmed. Source: NICE NG145 Thyroid disease: assessment and management, 2019 (updated 2023).

Sound: safety first, summon help, then de-escalate and look for organic causes (NICE NG10 principles; NG10 is written mainly for mental health and emergency settings but the principles apply). Key was longest: shortened.

options.C: Ensure everyone's safety first, calling security if needed

edits.why_correct: When there is an immediate threat of violence, safety comes first: keep a safe distance and exit route, move others away, and summon help such as security. Once the situation is safe, verbal de-escalation and assessment for underlying causes such as pain, delirium, hypoxia or withdrawal can follow. Source: NICE NG10 Violence and aggression: short-term management, 2015.

options.C: Document the latex allergy and arrange a latex-free theatre

edits.why_correct: Her history describes an immediate, IgE-mediated latex allergy with features of anaphylaxis. The allergy must be documented prominently and the theatre team informed, so that her procedure can be done in a latex-free environment with latex-free equipment throughout her care. This minimises the risk of a life-threatening perioperative reaction. Source: Association of Anaesthetists, Suspected anaphylactic reactions associated with anaesthesia, 2009; RCoA NAP6 report, 2018.

Sound: NICE CG89 1.1.6 lists scalds in a glove or stocking distribution, symmetrical limb scalds and sharply delineated borders as indicating forced immersion. Key was longest (E nearly equal): shortened.

options.C: Treat the scald, document findings and follow safeguarding procedures

edits.why_correct: A glove or sock pattern with a clear tide line and no splash marks suggests forced immersion rather than an accidental scald, and the delay in presentation adds to the concern. The child needs proper burns care and pain relief now, alongside careful documentation and referral through local safeguarding procedures, typically involving the paediatric team and children's social care. Source: NICE CG89 Child maltreatment: when to suspect maltreatment in under 18s, 2009 (updated 2025).

issues: Diagnosis correct. why_correct said 'stop, remove the cannula, elevate' while the pearl says to aspirate before removal for a vesicant: made consistent. Key was longest: shortened. Reviewer note: source is the Royal Marsden Manual extravasation entry (subscription; checked via search summary only).

options.B: Leakage of fluid into surrounding tissue

edits.why_correct: Local pain, cool pale swelling around the cannula and a slowing infusion are typical of fluid escaping into the subcutaneous tissue. This is infiltration if the fluid is non-irritant, or extravasation if it is a vesicant drug. The infusion should be stopped at once; for a vesicant, aspiration through the cannula is attempted before it is removed, then the limb is elevated and local extravasation guidance followed. Source: Royal Marsden Manual of Clinical Nursing Procedures, extravasation management (peripheral cannula), online edition 2024.
edits.correct_answer: B. Leakage of fluid into surrounding tissue

issues: Sound: positive identification with two identifiers, explanation and consent; written consent is not needed for cannulation; a nurse cannot consent for an adult. Key was longest: shortened.

options.B: Check her identity against wristband and chart, explain and seek consent

edits.why_correct: Positive patient identification using at least two identifiers checked against the wristband and the prescription prevents wrong-patient procedures, and bed numbers are not reliable identifiers. Drowsiness does not remove the need to explain and seek consent: she is rousable and may well be able to agree. If she genuinely lacked capacity, the doctor would act in her best interests under the Mental Capacity Act, not rely on a third party. Source: GMC Decision making and consent, 2020.
edits.correct_answer: B. Check her identity against wristband and chart, explain and seek consent

issues: Duplicate: u74-g05 PAN344 (third attendance in two months, burn, different accounts each time -> recognise pattern and follow safeguarding procedures); also live PED040.
Sound (objective, contemporaneous safeguarding records with the child's words verbatim). Key was longest: shortened.

options.E: Record the marks objectively, the boy's exact words, her assessment and actions

edits.why_correct: Safeguarding records must be accurate, factual and made at the time. They should describe injuries objectively (size, shape, colour, site, ideally with a body map), quote the child's words verbatim, give the clinician's assessment and record decisions and who was contacted. These records may later support multi-agency decisions or court proceedings, so opinion and conclusions should be kept separate from facts. Source: GMC Good medical practice, 2024 (paragraphs 69-70); NICE CG89 Child maltreatment, 2009 (updated 2025).
edits.correct_answer: E. Record the marks objectively, the boy's exact words, her assessment and actions

options.D: Record now the options and risks discussed, his questions and his choice

edits.why_correct: Notes should be made at the time or as soon as possible afterwards, and should record which options were offered, the material risks discussed, the patient's questions and his decision. This supports continuity of care, shows that consent was informed and reflects GMC guidance on decision making and consent. A vague summary or a delayed letter does not show what he was told. Source: GMC Decision making and consent, 2020; GMC Good medical practice, 2024.
edits.correct_answer: D. Record now the options and risks discussed, his questions and his choice

options.E: Findings and diagnosis now, with the reasoning added later only if a complaint is made

edits.why_correct: A good record lets another clinician understand what was found, why a decision was made and what the patient was told. For a headache that is managed in the community, documenting relevant negatives such as normal neurology and no meningism shows serious causes were considered, and recording safety-netting advice shows what to do if things change. GMC Good medical practice expects clear, accurate and timely records. Source: GMC Good medical practice, 2024 (paragraphs 69-70).
edits.correct_answer: C. History, examination with relevant negatives, reasoning, plan and safety-netting

issues: reinstated: partner g05 PAN5788 dropped. Full recheck: no repeat in live or held banks or kept items (live BX006 and u74-g04 PAQ12478 test correcting an erroneous entry, a different learning point). Clinically sound: a late entry is acceptable if clearly marked as retrospective, dated and timed when written and stating when the events occurred; backdating, inserting text among earlier entries or having someone else write it is misleading. Key was longest: shortened. Source added.

options.D: Write a new entry now marked as retrospective, timed now, stating when events occurred

edits.why_correct: Records must be honest and transparent. A late entry is acceptable as long as it is clearly identified as retrospective, signed, and dated and timed when it was actually written, while stating when the events occurred. Inserting text so it looks contemporaneous, or having someone else author it, would be misleading and could be a probity issue. Source: GMC Good medical practice, 2024 (paragraphs 69-70); MDU guidance on effective record keeping.
edits.correct_answer: D. Write a new entry now marked as retrospective, timed now, stating when events occurred

Sound (next of kin has no right to a competent adult's information; ask the patient). Key was longest: shortened the key and lengthened C. Reviewer note: related to live BX952 (explicit refusal, partner asks), but here the patient has not yet been asked and the learning point is to seek his agreement; kept, though a reviewer may judge it too close.

options.E: Explain he cannot share it without his father's agreement and offer to ask him
options.C: Share the result once the son signs a form promising to keep it strictly private

edits.why_correct: The father is a competent adult, so information about his scan belongs to him and should not be passed to relatives without his consent or another lawful justification. Nothing here suggests a risk to others or a legal requirement to disclose. The doctor can be courteous, explain the position and offer to check with the patient when he wakes, which respects confidentiality while supporting the family. Source: GMC Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information, 2017.
edits.correct_answer: E. Explain he cannot share it without his father's agreement and offer to ask him

issues: Duplicate: live BX952 (competent patient refuses sharing with partner; partner rings surgery -> maintain confidentiality unless justified). Same scenario and learning point.
Sound (GMC: consent needed before disclosing to employers; Access to Medical Reports Act 1988 pearl correct). Key was longest: shortened.

options.D: Decline unless the patient consents or disclosure is otherwise justified

edits.why_correct: The patient is a competent adult who has asked that his workplace is not told about his illness. An employer has no right to medical information without the patient's consent, and there is no safety risk to others or legal requirement that would justify disclosure. The GP should decline and can suggest that the employer seeks consent through a formal occupational health referral. Source: GMC Confidentiality: disclosing information for employment, insurance and similar purposes, 2017.
edits.correct_answer: D. Decline unless the patient consents or disclosure is otherwise justified

edits.why_correct: Young people aged 16 and 17 are presumed to have capacity to consent to their own treatment, and they are owed the same duty of confidentiality as adults. He clearly understands and weighs the information, and there are no safeguarding concerns. His wish that his parents are not told should therefore be respected, with disclosure only if there were a risk of serious harm to him or others. Source: GMC 0-18 years: guidance for all doctors, 2007 (updated 2024).
